title: Control at 30 Hz, not 50
question: How fast can the policy act on the real arm?
conclusion: 30 Hz. The servo bus is half-duplex serial shared by five servos on a non-realtime OS, and 30 Hz is what it sustains. At 1.8 m/s the ball moves 60 mm between decisions, against a 35 mm usable blade radius, so training randomises the rate over 30-60 Hz rather than assuming one.

title: Paying per bounce teaches a dribble
question: Why did v1 score 63 bounces yet look wrong?
conclusion: A reward per bounce is maximised by tiny, fast bounces (an 8 cm dribble). From v3 on the reward is seconds of good flight, with an apex band of 20-35 cm.

title: A policy trained at one rate fails at another
question: Does a 60 Hz policy work at 30 Hz?
conclusion: No: v2 made 58.6 bounces at 60 Hz and 5.6 at 30 Hz. The control period is now an input and is randomised in training.

title: v3-v6 are within noise of each other; v5 leads
question: Which version is best, under identical conditions?
conclusion: Fresh evaluation, 30 randomised drops each, held-out seed, 60 s limit: v5 kept 70% up for the full minute, v3/v4/v6 57%, v7 43% (its last checkpoint landed on a dip). Where the ball is dropped matters most: within 12 cm of the centre about 60% reach the limit, 20-40 cm out none do.

title: The 'weak, jammed' arm was a 5 V supply
question: Why could the shoulder not lift the arm?
conclusion: The STS3215s are the 12 V version and were on 5 V. On the ~13 V supply the lift moves at 3-13% load.

title: The real servos lag the sim's by 0.1-0.27 s
question: How closely does the real arm follow a sim episode?
conclusion: At real time, typical errors are 1-11 degrees and 0.07-0.27 s behind, worst at the elbow and base. Peak load stays near 25%, so the limit is servo response, not torque. A policy trained on the sim arm expects a much faster arm; the actuator model needs the measured response.

title: One camera cannot fit its lens and its pose together
question: Why did the blue-paddle camera calibration give 3-36 cm errors?
conclusion: Fitting focal length and camera pose from the same sightings is ill-conditioned: fits ranged 53-104 degrees of field of view. So the lens is now measured separately (ChArUco board), and the pose from STag markers on the paddle.

title: A white ball is fragile under changing light; orange is not
question: How does the detector hold up under relit conditions?
conclusion: The white ball was found in only 15-57% of frames under re-lit conditions (backlit, warm, dim). The orange-ball detector, using vividness after white balance, finds it in all 10 conditions and ignores the same-hue wooden table.

title: Off-centre, a ball looks up to 5% bigger
question: Why was the ball's depth 10-20 mm off in the sim?
conclusion: Away from the image centre a sphere images as an ellipse, stretched and shifted outward. The old on-axis formula took that as the ball being nearer. CameraModel now inverts the exact outline (a conic), which brought the ball position to about 1 mm.

title: The detector reads the outline ~0.3 px small
question: What is left after the exact sphere model?
conclusion: A constant ~0.3 px under-read of the radius, from mixed pixels at the edge: 1% of the radius, 5 mm of depth at half a metre. It is calibrated out from the ball resting on the table, where its centre is exactly 20 mm up and the camera ray alone fixes its distance.

title: A free 14-coefficient lens fit trades the image centre for prism and tilt
question: Why did the sim lens fit put the image centre 25-74 px off?
conclusion: The thin-prism and sensor-tilt terms can stand in for a shifted centre, so a free fit drifts even when started at the truth. Fitting in stages (5, then 8 coefficients, then 12 and 14 with the centre held) brings it within 1-2 px, with sub-pixel fits throughout.

title: MuJoCo's principal point has the opposite sign to OpenCV's
question: How do we render exactly an OpenCV camera in MuJoCo?
conclusion: principal_pixel is an offset from the image centre with the opposite sign to OpenCV's, and MuJoCo pixel centres sit at +0.5. With that, a render matches an OpenCV projection to 0.04 px. sim.cameras.add_cv_camera does it.

title: What the hand-eye fit cannot tell apart
question: Which arm errors can the paddle markers measure?
conclusion: Everything except two, and neither changes where the paddle ends up: a shoulder-pan offset is indistinguishable from the camera turning about the base, and the paddle turned on the wrist about the roll axis is a wrist-roll offset. A marker on the base (id 2) would pin the first.

title: STag markers need the reference generator's clean-up passes
question: Why did the printed markers have slivers?
conclusion: Drawing the code, filler and blank circles over one another leaves thin crescents and flecks; the reference generator removes them with five majority-vote passes and redraws the circles. The port now includes them. A marker that decodes is not necessarily a correct marker.

title: A colour step on the bed face must stay under half a layer
question: How can each colour be its own surface without spoiling a face-down print?
conclusion: On the face against the bed, a step deeper than half the first layer (0.1 mm of 0.2) leaves the recessed colour printing over air. 0.08 mm there, 0.1 mm on faces that print upward.

title: The back marker's edge can merge with the connector
question: Why do ~1 in 30 calibration views read a corner wrong?
conclusion: Seen at an angle, the back marker's black edge runs into the black connector and its shadow; and a marker cut off by the frame still decodes with its lost corners guessed. Both are rejected: no corner within 12 px of the frame edge, and views worse than 3x the median are dropped before a refit.
